solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Democrats after review accepting old people, important, may move in these (10)

definitions.text: people, important, may move in these

indicators.note: a text after review has been reworked, so its letters are rearranged
the rearranged letters take the O inside them

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Party members rethink their stance while taking in the elderly vote.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole second half reads as a comment on voters, but it is the definition: a motorcade is the convoy important people travel in.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorcade is a procession of cars carrying dignitaries, so VIPs move in motorcades.

clue.text: To some extent likes the rackety girl (6)

indicators.note: only part of the following words is used, so the answer sits inside them

explanation.surface: Someone half-admits to a fondness for a noisy young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts in the last letters of 'likes', so the break between words hides the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Esther is a female first name, borne by the biblical queen, and crosswords use 'girl' for any such name.

clue.text: Note about dance at home – no palms beyond this? (4,4)

indicators.note: the note goes around the other pieces

blocks.note: te, a variant of ti, the seventh note of the sol-fa scale
a reel is a lively Scottish dance

explanation.surface: A musician wonders where the palm-lined dance floor ends.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: above the tree line no trees grow at all, so certainly no palms, though palms are not the trees one finds near it.
explanation.definitionFit: The tree line is the altitude or latitude limit beyond which trees, palms included, cannot survive the cold.

clue.text: Not exactly politician’s military life (4)

blocks.note: MP, Member of Parliament; the 's reads as 'is'

explanation.surface: A description of a politician's past service in the armed forces, slightly embellished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not exactly' looks like a hedge about the politician's honesty, but it stands for CA, the abbreviation for circa.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers are housed in tents or barracks at an army base, so going to camp stands for the soldiering existence as a whole.

clue.text: Row about Maine’s abbreviation – look up and watch maybe (10)

indicators.note: the row goes around the other pieces
in a down clue, up means read from the bottom, so PEEK turns round

blocks.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Maine

explanation.surface: Instructions for finding a state's abbreviation in a table, then checking the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a verb joined to 'look up', but it is a noun, and 'maybe' marks it as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A watch keeps time, so it is one kind of timekeeper.

clue.text: Popular group fly perhaps (6)

blocks.note: a sect is a group, especially a religious one

explanation.surface: A fashionable band that might just take off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popular group' reads as a pop band, and 'fly' as a verb; 'perhaps' marks the fly as an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the housefly is a six-legged winged creature, and 'perhaps' warns that it stands for the whole class.

clue.text: No mixer – learner, individual needing smooth progress on way up (4,4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from the bottom, so FLOW turns round

blocks.note: L for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: A shy beginner who needs things to go smoothly as they climb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No mixer' is the definition: someone who does not mix socially, not something missing from a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixer is a sociable person who circulates at parties; the solitary type who prefers their own company, like a wolf hunting apart from the pack, is not.

clue.text: From metallics and others (2,2)

indicators.note: the answer is taken from within the next word

explanation.surface: A list of metallic paints and other colours.
explanation.walkthrough: ET AL is Latin et alii, used at the end of a list of names.
explanation.definitionFit: Et al is short for et alii, Latin for 'and others'.

clue.text: Eyeing from here, proves boat is not manoeuvring? (11,4)

indicators.note: the letters are moved about into a new position

explanation.surface: A watcher on shore concludes that a boat is not moving.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a lookout's report; 'not manoeuvring' seems to describe the boat, but 'not' is fodder and 'manoeuvring' the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An observation post is a place from which one keeps watch.

clue.text: Expression of contempt about colour (5)

blocks.note: och, a Scottish and Irish exclamation of impatience or scorn

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at a choice of colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like an instruction to wrap one piece around another, but here it simply supplies letters, as the Latin-derived word used in business letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the earthy yellow-brown pigment made from iron-rich clay gives its name to that shade.

clue.text: Reportedly quiet before lunch, say, patchy (9)

indicators.note: as heard, so the word for quiet is taken by its sound

blocks.note: peace = quiet; piece sounds the same
lunch is an example of a meal

explanation.surface: Someone wants some peace before lunch, though the arrangements are uneven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' covers only the quiet part; MEAL is taken as it stands, and 'say' marks lunch as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done piecemeal is done bit by bit, unevenly, hence patchy.

clue.text: He takes meat in refurbished Rio cavern (9)

indicators.note: renovated, so the letters are made over into a new order

explanation.surface: A man dines on meat in a done-up cave restaurant in Rio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as a location in the surface, but it only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A flesh-eating animal, such as a lion, lives on meat; 'he takes' is the setter's personal way of saying 'one who eats'.

clue.text: Overnight case? No (10)

blocks.note: reads as a small suitcase for one night away; the setter means a hospital case, a patient
the patient is not kept overnight

explanation.surface: A question about a small suitcase, answered in the negative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overnight case' suggests luggage, but the case is a medical one; a patient who does not stay overnight in hospital is an outpatient.
explanation.definitionFit: An outpatient is treated at hospital without being admitted overnight.

clue.text: After tips from teetotaller rejected fish (5)

indicators.note: the tips of a word are its first and last letters
the rejected part comes after the tips

blocks.note: out = rejected, as a proposal thrown out

explanation.surface: A fish sent back after a non-drinker's advice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' reads as advice from the teetotaller, but it means the end letters of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the speckled freshwater species prized by anglers belongs to the salmon family.

clue.text: Frankly discuss story finally changed with support of country (4,6)

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is swapped for another
in a down clue, the support goes underneath

blocks.note: story = TALE, with its last letter changed to K

explanation.surface: Someone speaks plainly after a tale's ending is altered, with a nation's backing.
explanation.walkthrough: The change is unguided: only the crossing letters, or the phrase itself, pin the new last letter as K.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the American phrase means to speak bluntly and get down to business, especially about money.

clue.text: On return, emphasised farmers’ body is in sharing arrangement – sweet (a bit perhaps) (15)

indicators.note: coming back means read the word backwards
the farmers' body goes inside the pool

blocks.note: a pool is an arrangement for sharing, such as a car pool
NFU, the National Farmers' Union, the body representing farmers in England and Wales

explanation.surface: A report on farm-union politics that ends up talking about pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' is the British word for dessert, and 'a bit perhaps' flags that the answer is only a portion of one.
explanation.definitionFit: A dessertspoonful is a small serving of pudding, a bit of sweet, as dessert is called in Britain.

clue.text: Back in Paris is becoming rigorous in the extreme (8)

blocks.note: the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone returns to Paris and grows strict.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in Paris' reads as a return to the city; the split is 'Back' then 'in Paris is'.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of an adjective meaning strict and severe, so 'in the extreme' supplies the -EST ending.

clue.text: Exaggerated merit of completed series’ introduction – out of date (8)

explanation.surface: A review praises a finished TV series' opening episode too much, now that it has dated.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition includes 'of': to oversell a thing is to exaggerate the merit of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversell something is to hype or talk it up beyond its real worth, so the past participle matches 'exaggerated merit of'.

clue.text: Perfume despatched, by sound of it (5)

indicators.note: judged by how it sounds, so the word is heard, not spelt

blocks.note: despatched = SENT, the past tense of send; say it and respell it

explanation.surface: Perfume has been posted off, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: SENT and SCENT sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a fragrant liquid dabbed on the skin goes by either name, and both also mean a pleasant smell.

clue.text: Unproved premise in article so idealistic, silly first of all (6)

indicators.note: take the first letter of each of the words before it

blocks.note: the first letters of So Idealistic Silly

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses an article's unproven premise as naive and silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First of all' seems to mean 'before anything else', but it asks for the first letter of all three words.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesis is a proposition put forward to be argued and defended, not yet established as true.

clue.text: A place for bowling impresses writer – time for correspondence (9)

indicators.note: to impress is to press into, so the green takes the writer inside

blocks.note: a bowling green, the lawn for playing bowls
the writer of a clue refers to themself as ME
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A bowling club impresses a visiting author, who later writes letters about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correspondence' pairs with 'writer' to suggest letters, but it means matching.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: when two accounts correspond they match up, tally or accord with each other.

clue.text: Describing position of summit, beginning to end (6)

indicators.note: the first letter moves to the end of the word

blocks.note: a height is a summit; move its H from the front to the back

explanation.surface: A climber explains where the summit stands, from start to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing position of' reads as a climber's phrase, but an ordinal like eighth describes position in a sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighth is an ordinal number, a word telling where something stands in a sequence, as in 'eighth in line'.

clue.text: Dined alone cut off in plant (9)

indicators.note: the last letter of 'alone' is cut away
the letters are off, out of place, so rearrange them

blocks.note: alone with its last letter cut

explanation.surface: Someone who ate by themselves was cut off from company in a factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a factory in the surface, but it is the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The dandelion is a common yellow-flowered plant.

clue.text: Read about challenge (4)

indicators.note: turned about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone studies up on a challenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read about' passes for 'research'; 'about' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, as nouns: daring someone to jump off a wall is issuing them a test of nerve.

clue.text: Type of light knee joint, nothing odd in that (4)

indicators.note: no odd-numbered letters of that phrase are kept, only the even ones

explanation.surface: A doctor shines a light on a knee joint and sees nothing unusual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing odd in that' reads as reassurance about the knee, but it tells you to drop the odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Neon lighting glows when current passes through the noble gas in a glass tube, as in shop signs.

clue.text: Coming back, make fun of our group? That’s annoying! (5)

indicators.note: returning, so the letters read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone complains when mockery of their group comes back at them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sugar!' is a mild exclamation, a polite stand-in for a ruder word.
explanation.definitionFit: Regional use: in Britain the word is a mild oath, a polite stand-in for a ruder expletive when irritated.

clue.text: Note usual triers messing about – dangerous game (7,8)

indicators.note: fooling around with the letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A coach notices the regular triallists fooling around, which is a risky business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' looks like a musical note or an instruction to observe, but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Russian roulette, spinning a revolver with one loaded chamber and firing at oneself, is a notoriously dangerous game.
